title: Microsoft's UK Regulatory Problem Just Got Bigger - TradingView
content: Microsoft Corp. (MSFT, Financials) the software and cloud behemoth, is facing a bigger legal battle in the U.K. than only cloud switching. Britain's Competition and Markets Authority recommended granting Microsoft strategic market status in commercial software. That might open the door to new restrictions governing how Microsoft packages products like Excel, Teams, security tools and Copilot. The regulator said Microsoft has a strong position in operating systems, productivity applications, security, servers and database administration. It also highlighted hurdles that make it hard to transfer providers. That's important because Microsoft's revenue model works better if users use more than one of its products. The more integrated those technologies are, the more difficult it may be for competing services to carve out a piece of the account. The CMA also aims to look into whether companies are allowed to use rival AI technologies with Copilot, and if Microsoft's licensing rules restrict cloud options. Microsoft disputed the regulator's stance, saying its products were open and interoperable. The danger to investors is not that it will be broken up or hit with a huge fine. It is the very potential of rules that erodes bundling benefits in the long run. The CMA's ultimate verdict, due in February, is next to watch. Select market data provided by ICE Data Services. title: Microsoft Makes a Massive Move to Secure Its AI Future - TradingView
content: NiSource NI shares rose after the utility signed a 20-year energy agreement with Microsoft MSFT to supply roughly 1,100 megawatts of new generation capacity beginning in 2028. The deal is another sign of just how much power Big Tech is securing for future data-center expansion. Under the agreement, NiSource's NIPSCO and GenCo units will provide the generation and transmission infrastructure needed to serve Microsoft's load while continuing to support existing customers in Indiana. Microsoft will fully fund the generation and transmission assets required for its data-center demand, according to the companies. That point matters because utilities across the U.S. are facing growing scrutiny over whether residential customers could end up subsidizing infrastructure built for hyperscale data centers. The new assets are also expected to strengthen NIPSCO's transmission system, improving grid reliability and resilience for existing customers. The agreement includes another major component: 600 MW of battery storage under a long-term tolling agreement with GenCo. The storage facility will be developed and constructed by an affiliate of AGP Group. NiSource said the Microsoft agreement increases expected savings for NIPSCO electric customers over the life of its data-center contracts to about $1.75 billion, up from the previously disclosed $1.4 billion. That could equate to savings of as much as $140 per customer annually. Shares of NiSource gained roughly 3% in early Friday trading following the announcement. I think the more important part of this deal is not simply the 1,100 MW headline. Microsoft is effectively underwriting the infrastructure required for its own demand, while NiSource gains a very large, long-duration customer without shifting the capital burden onto existing ratepayers. That could make the agreement a useful template for utilities trying to capture AI-driven electricity demand without creating political or regulatory backlash. For investors, the key things to watch are project execution, regulatory approvals, returns on invested capital, transmission expansion and whether NiSource signs additional hyperscaler agreements. If more data-center customers are willing to directly fund the infrastructure they require, AI-related load growth could become a much cleaner earnings opportunity for regulated utilities. title: MSFT Stock Falls to $525 after Failing at the Highs, as Regulation and Spending Concerns Mount - FXLeaders
content: Microsoft shares have reversed from above $550 toward $525 after failing to reach a record high, as a UK regulatory investigation, intensifying competition and massive infrastructure spending raise questions about the sustainability of its growth. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) shares fell 2.45% on Friday, extending their weekly decline after failing to establish a new record above $550. The stock has since retreated toward $525, reversing gains that followed news of the company’s custom-chip development. The pullback reflects several pressures confronting the technology giant, including increased regulatory scrutiny in the UK, rising competition in productivity software and questions about whether enormous infrastructure investments will generate sufficient returns. Although Microsoft’s cloud and software businesses remain substantial growth drivers, investors are increasingly focused on the costs required to maintain that expansion. The UK’s Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) concluded an investigation launched in May 2026 into Microsoft’s software business, including products such as Word, Excel and Teams. The watchdog believes Microsoft should be designated as having strategic market status, potentially giving regulators greater powers to investigate its conduct and impose targeted interventions. The CMA’s concerns include the difficulty customers may face when switching away from Microsoft’s products and the company’s position among approximately 20 million UK users. Its Copilot offering has also attracted scrutiny over the competitive challenges it may create for rival providers. The proposed designation does not automatically establish wrongdoing, but additional regulatory intervention could create compliance costs and potentially affect Microsoft’s pricing and product-bundling strategies. Microsoft’s Maia 300 processor highlights its efforts to improve computing efficiency and reduce dependence on external chip suppliers. The processor reportedly targets 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU systems, while its 96-accelerator configuration is designed to deliver up to seven times the rack-scale throughput of Maia 200. Custom silicon could help Microsoft manage computing costs, although developing and deploying these systems requires substantial investment. The company may also seek additional computing capacity from SpaceX. According to The Information, the two companies discussed leasing computing capacity during the summer, although the current status of those talks remains unclear. SpaceX expects to finish 2026 with slightly more than 2 gigawatts of computing capacity and aims to expand to between 5 GW and 10 GW next year. Meanwhile, Microsoft continues to face capacity constraints despite plans for approximately $175 billion in capital spending during 2026. Microsoft shares jumped above the critical $500 level as they rebounded strongly in the last 2 months, climb above $550 earlier this week but slipped below $530 again. The price slip tested the 20 daily SMA in gray in September which has been acting as support. The $550 area represents both psychological and technical resistance so for now MAFT buyers gave up at this zone. Microsoft’s stock has undergone a notable repricing in recent months, signaling a broader reset in how investors are assessing mega-cap technology leaders. After peaking above $555 in October 2025, shares retreated sharply, and despite the revival in 2026, buyers haven’t been able to break above that level. Microsoft’s financial results remain strong. Fiscal 2026 revenue increased 18% to $331.8 billion, while net income rose 31% to $133.7 billion. However, capital expenditure reached $41 billion in the fiscal fourth quarter, with roughly two-thirds allocated to shorter-lived CPUs and GPUs. Operating cash flow was $55.4 billion, but free cash flow came in at $19.6 billion. Capital expenditure is expected to remain above $50 billion per quarter during fiscal 2027. These figures highlight the financial burden of expanding infrastructure. The key question is whether demand and revenue can grow quickly enough to justify these commitments without putting sustained pressure on cash generation. Microsoft is also restructuring its gaming business, with approximately 3,200 job reductions planned during fiscal 2027, including 1,600 immediate cuts. Further reported reductions highlight efforts to improve efficiency across the division. Meanwhile, Google Workspace is intensifying competition in productivity software, as customers reassess Microsoft 365 pricing and bundled features. Microsoft’s long-term prospects remain supported by its enterprise software, cloud infrastructure and custom-chip development. However, regulatory pressure, competition and elevated spending complicate the outlook. With shares retreating toward $525, buyers need to demonstrate that the recent reversal is temporary. A sustained recovery will depend on continued earnings growth and evidence that infrastructure investments can deliver attractive returns. The $665 price target mentioned by analysts offers potential upside, but reaching it will require Microsoft to justify its spending commitments while navigating mounting competitive and regulatory risks.

title: UK proposes 'strategic market status' for Microsoft; final decision set for February - TradingView
content: Following months of investigation, the U.K.'s Competition and Markets Authority has proposed to designate Microsoft MSFT with "strategic market status" regarding its business software ecosystem. "SMS designation does not find or assume wrongdoing," the decision reads. "Instead, it is the gateway into the UK's digital markets competition regime. It enables the CMA to take action aimed at promoting competition in technology sectors that are key to UK consumers, businesses and the economy." The CMA will now conduct consultation through November 13, and it will issue a final decision on the proposed designation by Feb. 13, 2027. "We welcome the CMA's acknowledgement that Microsoft's market position in cloud does not justify a Digital Markets Competition Regime designation but do not share the CMA's views in its proposed decision on business software solutions," a Microsoft spokesperson said to Seeking Alpha. "All our products—including Copilot—are open and interoperable, giving customers the ability to use them alongside competing services and choose solutions that work best for them at attractive prices. We will continue engaging constructively to ensure UK customers and businesses carry on benefiting from robust competition." The CMA concludes in its report that Microsoft's broad suite of business software products work well together, and its bundling options offer enterprise-wide discounts for customers. "A broad range of UK customers tell us that these commercial and integration benefits are an important driver for their decision to buy Microsoft business software products," the CMA said. "This has allowed Microsoft to use a position of strength with customers in one product area to expand into others. As an example, Microsoft added security products to the bundles that included its productivity software applications, as security grew in importance for business software customers." However, they also concluded that the success of its bundling efforts makes it difficult for competitors. "Even rivals who offer products across more than one digital activity face challenges in winning customers from Microsoft," the report noted. "Their narrower product range, disadvantages due to network effects and significant customer switching costs limit their ability to compete for existing Microsoft customers, many of which are large enterprises." If the CMA confirms the designation, its actions include supporting customer choice and enabling innovation. Its new 20-year agreement for the planned campus is expected to contribute to a broader strategy that NiSource says could deliver $1.75 billion in savings to existing electricity customers. “Affordability is not separate from economic development; it is a key pillar of our GenCo model,” NiSource CEO Lloyd Yates said, adding that the company aims to attract investment and create jobs while protecting existing customers. title: NiSource gains on 20-year Microsoft energy agreement for 1,100 MW - TradingView
content: NiSource NI signed a 20-year energy agreement with Microsoft MSFT to supply about 1,100 MW of new generation capacity starting in 2028, sending shares 3% higher in early trading on Friday. The GenCo-owned pool portfolio will be increased by ~1,100 MW with NIPSCO and GenCo to provide transmission and generation infrastructure to ensure adequate assets to serve Microsoft’s data center and NIPSCO’s customers while providing a safe, reliable, and coordinated power supply. In connection with the Microsoft agreement, GenCo has contracted 600 MW of battery storage under a long-term tolling agreement. The facility will be developed and constructed by an affiliate of AGP Group. Microsoft fully funds all generation and transmission required to serve its load. These assets will upgrade NIPSCO’s electric transmission system, improving grid reliability and resilience for customers in the state of Indiana, while ensuring current residential and business customers are protected from the costs of serving the data center, the companies said. The agreement builds on the previously disclosed $1.4B expected customer savings over the life of data center customer contracts, increasing total expected NIPSCO electric customer savings to approximately $1.75B, equating to as much as $140 per customer annually. title: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella Just Shared Bad News for Nvidia and Great News for This Rival Chipmaker - The Motley Fool
content: New plans for Azure could leave less room for Nvidia. Microsoft (MSFT -1.93%) is planning a big change to its Azure cloud computing data centers starting next year. It will rely much more on its custom-designed silicon than on leading graphics processing units (GPUs) like those from Nvidia (NVDA -1.43%). It's already made significant progress in expanding workloads for its Maia 200 chips, and it expects its next-generation Maia 300 chips to deliver significant improvements when it starts deploying them next year. "Starting next calendar year, we will scale our Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments, making it the primary inference system for our own product and services," CEO Satya Nadella said.  That's great news for its custom chip partner, Marvell Technology (MRVL -5.56%), and bad news for Nvidia. Nvidia's extreme dominance of the data center GPU space during the first few years of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom left its market share with nowhere to go but down. Its biggest customers, including the hyperscalers and leading AI frontier labs, have developed custom solutions that can handle AI workloads, and that can deliver better price performance on specific tasks than Nvidia's GPUs. That said, GPUs offer far greater flexibility in terms of the types of tasks they can perform, making them particularly valuable for companies deploying servers to sell compute capacity to third parties with dynamic demands. Notice that Microsoft is starting its Maia expansion by focusing on its own products and services, not on leasing Maia compute capacity to third parties looking to cut costs on their OpenAI GPT-based applications. Their use, though, could expand over the long run. Alphabet (GOOG -2.32%) (GOOGL -2.47%), which has been building its own custom AI chips for longer than any of its competitors, has seen strong adoption of its Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) by its Google Cloud customers for training and inference. Apple used TPUs to train Apple Intelligence, and Anthropic is using gigawatts worth of TPUs to develop its large language models. While Nvidia can continue to grow sales extremely quickly, other chipmakers' growth rates are likely to outpace it. That's reflected in its P/E valuation, which now sits below those of its biggest rivals. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » During its 2026 investor day this month, Marvell said it expects that it will grow its share of the custom AI accelerator market over the next five years. Its work on the Maia 300 is likely a big reason why. Microsoft's plan to make that processor the primary inference system for its products and services is in line with earlier reports that it will make a big step up in custom silicon orders starting next year. The revenue opportunity for Marvell is huge. Microsoft will spend approximately $175 billion in capital expenditures on data centers over the next year. Roughly two-thirds of that will go toward servers and networking equipment. If Marvell takes just a sliver of that spending, it would amount to a huge boost to its revenue, which totaled just $9.5 billion over the last four quarters. Marvell believes the combination of its custom AI chips and its networking chips will help it grow revenue tenfold over the next five years. That is to say, Microsoft's ramp-up in Maia chips is just the start. Marvell also signed a deal with Google earlier this year to design and sell inference-optimized versions of its TPU chips. The deal also gives Alphabet the option to take a stake in Marvell. Considering Marvell's growth potential, the stock's forward P/E of 63 looks inexpensive. If you look out to its fiscal 2029 (which mostly takes place in calendar 2028), the stock trades at just 21 times earnings estimates. Given its potential to capture a significant slice of the market for data center AI processors, that seems like a good price to pay. title: Microsoft AI chief says the company beat OpenAI at its own game, using a quarter of the computing power - Business Insider
content: Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman told employees an in-house model was better than a similar offering from OpenAI, one of the software giant's biggest customers and partners. "We now have a stronger pre-trained base model than the model that currently powers GPT 5.6 Sol," Suleyman said during a town hall meeting with employees on Thursday. "And in fact, we used one-quarter of the compute that OpenAI used to train their model." Pre-training is the first stage of building an AI model, when it learns patterns from huge amounts of text, images, and other information. This takes massive amounts of expensive computing power, so Microsoft could save money if it's worked out a way to do this more efficiently. Microsoft announced the model, MAI-Base-2, earlier on Thursday. Suleyman said Microsoft privately tested this model against OpenAI models, including one nicknamed "Spud" that powers GPT-5.6. He added that Microsoft's model performed better on tests measuring how well AI can understand and predict patterns in information. The comparisons are based on technical information Microsoft has about OpenAI's models, Suleyman said. "Privately and confidentially, we've also compared it to the OpenAI models," Suleyman told employees, while suggesting that Microsoft has special access to information on how OpenAI models perform. It's notable that Suleyman would choose to highlight limitations of OpenAI models, even in private discussions. Microsoft has invested billions of dollars in OpenAI, and owns a stake in the startup that is likely worth more than $100 billion. Any criticism of OpenAI could potentially dent the value of this huge investment. The two companies also have a major partnership, with Microsoft offering OpenAI models to its Azure cloud customers. Microsoft has used OpenAI models for its own products such as Copilot, too. Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get. Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters. But the relationship between the two companies has frayed in the past year or so. Increasingly, Microsoft has tried to branch out from OpenAI, including by working on its own models. Suleyman also said Microsoft's new AI model used "12 times less computation than was used for DeepSeek, for example, on compute efficiency." Suleyman didn't specify which DeepSeek model, but a public blog post described the pre-training of MAI-Base-2 being a lot more efficient than a similar offering from the Chinese lab, called DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Base. Microsoft in March created a new combined team for its commercial and consumer Copilot products and reassigned Suleyman to focus on building AI models in the company's superintelligence unit. Microsoft declined to comment and OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment on Thursday. Have a tip? title: Morgan Stanley finds a new twist in Microsoft's AI story - Yahoo Finance Australia
content: Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results Everyone has been watching the wrong race. While the AI world obsesses over which lab builds the best model, a fresh CIO survey from Morgan Stanley points to a quieter fight playing out beneath the surface, one Microsoft may already be winning. In a note shared with TheStreet on Oct. 12, Morgan Stanley published findings from its third-quarter 2026 AlphaWise CIO survey. The bank maintained its Overweight rating and $600 price target on Microsoft, against a closing price of $541.15 that day. But the more telling data was not about the stock. It was about where enterprise IT chiefs think AI money is actually heading. Also read: Wall Street doubles down on Microsoft stock for investors One of the more interesting questions Morgan Stanley threw into this survey was about AI orchestration. Not which model do you use, but who sits above the models, directing traffic, managing data permissions, keeping an eye on costs. Microsoft pulled 20% of responses on that one. LLM providers collectively were right behind at 17%. Google got 5%, Amazon 4%. That finding runs counter to the popular narrative. The assumption has been that whoever wins the model race wins the enterprise AI race. But a growing number of companies are spreading workloads across multiple models rather than committing to one. The moment a business is running different models for different tasks, it needs something above the models to keep things organized. That is the orchestration layer, and right now Microsoft is where most CIOs say they'd go for it. Microsoft's setup for this is Azure at the infrastructure level, Fabric for enterprise data, Foundry to select and route AI tasks, and Copilot to surface the results inside everyday applications. A company could run a competitor's model through that stack and Microsoft still collects on the infrastructure, the data layer, and the software. Three revenue opportunities from one AI workflow. Thirty percent of CIOs named Microsoft as the vendor most likely to capture the biggest share of generative AI spending in 2026, up from 27% the prior quarter, according to the survey. LLM providers came in at 16%, Google at 8%, Amazon at 7%. Pull back to a three-year horizon and things get messier. Microsoft is at 28%, which was 30% just last quarter. LLM providers climbed from 17% to 21% in that same window. The vendor consolidation story that once looked inevitable hasn't materialized. Companies are running multiple models, and the labs behind those models are now showing up in procurement conversations they weren't part of a year ago. You could read that as bad news for Microsoft. Morgan Stanley doesn't see it that way. Juggling several models creates its own headaches, and someone has to build the tooling that keeps everything organized. That is the business Foundry is going after. Here is something that should give AI bulls pause. Forty-two percent of CIOs told Morgan Stanley they cannot yet measure the returns on their AI token spending. Another 28% say returns are running below what they spend. Only 13% are ahead. Businesses are not waiting around on this. Forty-three percent already have token spend controls in place. Another 31% said they're putting them in before the end of 2027. Add those up and you're looking at most of the enterprise market actively trying to get a grip on what AI is actually costing them. The implication for Microsoft is straightforward. A tool that helps a company route cheaper models for simpler tasks and save the expensive ones for work that actually needs them has a pretty clear value proposition when IT chiefs are being asked to justify every dollar. That is Foundry's pitch, and the survey data suggests the appetite for it is growing. On the cloud side, 79% of surveyed CIOs said their organizations use Azure, ahead of AWS at 66% and Google Cloud at 43%. That maps closely to broader market data showing Azure holding the second largest share of global cloud infrastructure spend behind AWS. Microsoft's net score for expected IT budget share gains in 2026 came in at plus 43%, compared with plus 26% for Amazon and plus 4% for Google. Over the next three years, that gap stays wide: Microsoft at plus 35%, Amazon at plus 11%. Microsoft's $665 target hinges on a new AI advantage Meta and Microsoft just sent employees a memo about Anthropic The caveat is the growth rate. CIOs who use Azure expect spending to grow 15% in 2026, down from 21% in last year's survey for 2025. AWS is right alongside at 15%, with Google Cloud at 12%. Microsoft is still the biggest cloud by usage, but the growth advantage it once had over Amazon is largely gone. The longer runway is in AI workloads themselves. CIOs in the survey put AI and machine learning at 3.8% of their cloud spending today. In three years, they expect that to hit 9.9%. If even half of that growth flows through Azure, the demand picture looks pretty different from what current growth rates suggest. Getting there is another question. CIO surveys are a snapshot of intentions. They are not contracts. A respondent who says Microsoft will get the biggest share of their AI budget in 2026 could face a CFO in January with a very different view. The orchestration preference data is especially early, given that Foundry is still a relatively new product. Morgan Stanley has a $600 price target on Microsoft, but the range around it tells the real story. Their bull case goes to $795. Their bear case drops to $250. A $545 gap between best and worst is a pretty honest admission of how much nobody actually knows. Survey data shows where CIOs say they want to spend. Whether that translates into the numbers Microsoft needs to justify its valuation is a different conversation entirely. What this survey really captures is a change in the question enterprises are asking. It used to be: Which AI model should we use? Now it's: Who keeps all our models working together? That fight doesn't get nearly the attention the model race does, but it might end up mattering more. And right now, when CIOs try to answer it, Microsoft is the name that comes up first. content: Microsoft MSFT is betting on a busy fall gaming slate to revive its Xbox business. Gears of War: E-Day launched on Oct. 6 for Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers, while Activision's Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 arrives on Oct. 23 across Xbox Series X|S, PC, Steam, Battle.net, PlayStation 5 and Nintendo Switch 2. Unlike earlier releases, Modern Warfare 4 will not be on Game Pass at launch, a shift that favors full-priced sales over subscription bundling. On Oct. 8, Microsoft also created XP, a new Xbox division focused on extending franchises beyond games, and appointed a new chief executive for Mojang and Minecraft. However, guidance points to a gradual recovery. For the first quarter of fiscal 2027, Microsoft expects Xbox content and services revenues to decline in the mid-single digits, with hardware revenues also falling year over year. More Personal Computing revenues are projected to be between $12.2 billion and $12.7 billion. Management still expects Xbox to return to growth in fiscal 2027 as it resets its content portfolio, platform and operations. Activision is already supporting profitability. In fourth-quarter fiscal 2026, More Personal Computing gross margin percentage expanded on lower amortization from the Activision acquisition. Yet Xbox revenues fell 10% year over year, as content and services declined 10% against a strong first-party comparable and hardware dropped 13%. Segment operating expenses rose 8%, partly reflecting Xbox impairment charges. For fiscal 2026, Xbox revenues declined $1.7 billion, or 7%. Content and services slipped 5%, partly offset by Game Pass growth, while hardware fell 29% on lower console volumes. The October releases and Call of Duty's premium launch model could support the anticipated second-half rebound in gaming. However, near-term revenues decline, ongoing restructuring costs and Xbox's roughly 5.5% share of Microsoft's $90 billion in fourth-quarter revenues suggest gaming alone is unlikely to be a major catalyst for the stock. When Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) reports again later this month, one line will draw more attention than the rest: how fast Azure grew. That's a lot of weight for a single business inside a company that also sells Windows, Office, Xbox, and LinkedIn. But Azure has earned the spotlight. Azure is Microsoft's cloud platform. Businesses rent its computing power, storage, and AI tools to run their own apps and models. They pay as they use it, so every new AI workload becomes recurring revenue. In fiscal 2026, Azure's revenue passed $100 billion for the first time, according to CEO Satya Nadella, a milestone that cements Microsoft's standing among the 10 Best Growth Stocks to Buy Now According to Billionaires. The catch is what it costs to keep that engine growing. Whether the stock looks fairly priced comes down to one thing: can Azure's growth keep outrunning the bill? Azure revenue jumped 43% in fiscal Q4 2026, the most recent quarter on the books. That helped lift the Intelligent Cloud segment to $39.3 billion, up 32%. Speed is only half the story, though. The stronger evidence of a moat sits in commercial remaining performance obligation (contracted revenue not yet recognized), which climbed 84% to $678 billion. Enterprise customers don't sign commitments that size with a provider they plan to leave, a massive backlog that cements Microsoft's top ranking on lists like the 10 Best Cloud Computing Stocks to Buy According to Billionaires. Microsoft's other advantage is distribution. Companies already living in Microsoft 365 are an easy sell for AI add-ons, and Microsoft 365 Copilot has topped 30 million paid seats, per Nadella. The broader Microsoft Cloud business brought in $59.3 billion in the quarter, up 27%. Fast growth doesn't mean much if margins buckle under it. In fiscal Q4, revenue and operating income both rose 18%, a sign the cloud boom isn't being bought with thinner profits yet. Earnings need one clarification. GAAP diluted EPS came in at $4.81, but that figure was lifted by net gains tied to Microsoft's OpenAI stake. Non-GAAP EPS of $4.74, up 23%, strips those out, so it's the cleaner read on the operating business. For the full fiscal year, non-GAAP EPS reached $17.28, up 22%. Not everything is humming. More Personal Computing revenue slipped 4%, with Xbox content and services down 10%. That just underlines how much of the story now rests on the cloud. This is the worry that won't go away, and if you own the stock, it's the one worth watching. Capital expenditures hit $35.8 billion in fiscal Q4, against $17.1 billion a year earlier. For the full year, spending reached $115.9 billion, up from $64.6 billion. Those data centers and chips will show up as depreciation for years, whether or not demand holds. If Azure growth cools while the spending keeps climbing, margins are where the pain would show first, a key risk that investors must weigh across the Top 10 AI Stocks That Will Skyrocket. The counterweight is that $678 billion order book. Microsoft isn't building on hope alone; much of the demand it's building for is already under contract. That doesn't erase the risk, but it shrinks it. At a forward P/E of 27.39, as of October 12, investors are paying $27.39 for every $1 of expected earnings. That's a premium to the sector's 22.87, but it's below Microsoft's own 5-year average of 30.50. Growth is what makes the premium defensible. Analysts expect EPS growth of 19.80% in 2028, which is solid for a company already this large. While value investors can find cheaper tech multiples, Microsoft's deep enterprise integration and Copilot expansion firmly position it among the 11 Best Agentic AI Stocks to Buy Right Now. The discount to its own history suggests the market is already pricing in some of the capex risk. That's a reasonable place for the stock to sit heading into the next report. Big-money sentiment has cooled slightly, with 273 hedge funds holding the stock in the most recent quarter, down from 282 in the prior one. Short interest is just 0.82% of the float, pointing to relatively limited bearish positioning. The evidence points to a cloud business with growing contracted demand and steady margins, priced below Microsoft's own historical norm. For long-term investors comfortable with heavy spending in exchange for cloud and AI exposure, the setup looks reasonable. What would change that picture is a sharp slowdown from Azure's 43% pace while capital spending keeps rising. If that happens, today's multiple would start to look a lot less forgiving. title: Should Microsoft Stock’s New High Stop You From Buying? - Trefis
content: Most investors apply one rule to a stock like Microsoft (MSFT): buy low and never at the top. Microsoft stock closed near its 52-week high on October 13, 2026, making it the wrong time to buy under that logic. Rather than asking whether the price is too high, market participants should examine the historical performance of Microsoft’s earlier highs. Does that rule hold for Microsoft? Microsoft stock is at a high because the company earns more than it did a year ago. The share price rose 6.4% before dividends over the past year, while net income for the twelve months to June 2026 rose 31.3%. Investors are actually paying less for that profit. The price-to-earnings multiple, which measures what investors pay for each dollar of profit, was 37.3 a year ago and is 30.2 now. That growth is clearest in the cloud business. Revenue from Azure and other cloud services grew 43% in fiscal Q4 2026, the quarter to June. Management noted on that quarter’s call that customer demand continues to exceed available capacity. If you have held Microsoft for years, your biggest question may be taxes, not whether to buy at a high. See how a tax-aware transition works. What Happened After Microsoft Stock’s Earlier Highs? Historical data answers the question of how often Microsoft stock rises in the year following a peak. Since October 2016, counting at most one high every six months, the stock has set 13 earlier 52-week highs with a full year after them. It was higher a year later after 12 of those instances. This table details each of those highs except the earliest, alongside where the stock stood a year later. Split-adjusted closing prices, dividends excluded. The middle result was a gain of 31.1% a year later. A buyer purchasing Microsoft at a high usually experienced a strong following year rather than a trading mistake. The data indicates otherwise for Microsoft. Buying on any trading day over the same years gave a middle gain of 30.2% a year later, just below the result after a high. The rule against buying at the top has not held for the company, making a high about as good a day to buy as any other. Buyers usually face a small dip, but not always. The worst result came after the June 2025 high. A buyer at that time was 12.0% down a year later. That is why the rule is not foolish. Yet the June 2025 high was also the only one after which the stock closed 20% or more below the buying price within the year. The expected dip is generally minimal. After a typical earlier high, Microsoft stock’s lowest close in the following year was 2.4% below the buying price.
